title: A JB condo now sells 60% below launch price. Is it a bargain?
videoTitle: ASKING SEAN #199 | PRICES OF JB APARTMENTS DROPPED 70%
excerpt: A 24-year-old in Singapore can buy a Danga Bay subsale launched at about RM1 million for RM380,000, with rent covering the loan. Sean calls it only an okay deal and suggests other options.

qa.asker: E, a viewer who wrote in by email
qa.context: E is 24, works in Singapore and earns about S$7,000 a month. He prefers subsales because he can negotiate and calculate the yield. He has found an 881 sq ft two-bedroom unit in a Danga Bay high-rise, launched at about RM1 million and now valued around RM470,000, and negotiated it down to RM380,000. It is tenanted at about RM1,700 to RM1,800, a yield of about 5.6%, but the developer has a poor reputation online, many units remain unsold, and the township is on reclaimed land.
qa.question: Is this a sensible buy, should he take a full loan and cash out the difference, and is this the right way to play the property game?
qa.answer: Among JB apartments it is an okay deal and he understands the risks, but Sean would look further. At 24, E could afford more risk: a landed home in JB, which still has room to appreciate, or a completed, sold-out project from another developer. He should also weigh keeping his savings in Singapore dollars.

reasons.title: Buying below launch price isn't the same as cheap
reasons.body: Buyers who paid RM1 million on a 90% loan may still owe RM700,000 to RM800,000 on units now worth RM380,000. That shows the risk of buying with no check of rents and surrounding prices; the launch price is no measure of value.

reasons.title: JB high-rise has little room to grow
reasons.body: With plenty of land and supply, even well-run JB condos see little capital gain. Many Malaysians working there would rather pay a bit more for a landed home than RM380,000 for an apartment.

reasons.title: Stigma and unsold stock affect resale
reasons.body: While the developer still has unsold units and a poor reputation, the market can't correct itself, and the next buyer's perception sets the selling price. Check who runs the mall and how the building is managed.

reasons.title: The currency is part of the return
reasons.body: Keeping money in Singapore dollars already gains against the ringgit. Advertised rents for small units or Airbnb are often marketing claims, so rely on the real long-term rents around the building.

actions: Compare this unit with completed, sold-out projects by other JB developers offering similar discounts.
Run the same rent-versus-instalment check on landed homes near the border, even if they cost about RM1,000 a month to hold.
Weigh the return in ringgit against keeping the capital in Singapore dollars.
If he buys, decide on the loan size by how much monthly shortfall he is comfortable with.
Look up complaints and the mall's management before committing.
qa.caveat: For an older, conservative investor who wants a unit that pays for itself with little risk, this deal makes more sense. Sean has no insight into the build quality or the reclaimed land, so E should check those himself.

sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #199. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as the viewer stated them in February 2023; prices and exchange rates have changed since.
